propositions.text: Applicant seeks judicial review of August 27, 2020 decision revoking citizenship under subsection 10(5) of Citizenship Act.
propositions.quote: The Applicant, Roko Netani Gucake, seeks judicial review of an August 27, 2020 decision made by a senior analyst at Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) as the delegate of the Minister (Delegate) pursuant to subsection 10(5) of the Citizenship Act RSC 1985, c. C-29 (the Act) revoking the Applicant’s Canadian citizenship (the Decision).

paragraphs.summary: Applicant seeks judicial review of August 27, 2020 citizenship revocation decision under subsection 10(5) of Citizenship Act, court states.

propositions.text: Delegate found Applicant obtained citizenship by false representation, fraud, or concealment by nondisclosure of conviction, residence, studies in Australia.
propositions.quote: The Delegate determined the Applicant had obtained Canadian citizenship by false representation, fraud, or by knowingly concealing material circumstances when they failed to disclose their criminal conviction, residence and studies in Australia in their application for permanent resident status.

paragraphs.summary: Delegate found Applicant obtained citizenship by false representation, fraud, or concealment by nondisclosure, court reports.

propositions.text: Applicant admits false representations but argues analyst failed to consider personal circumstances warranting relief from revocation.
propositions.quote: The Applicant acknowledged the false representations, but argues that the analyst failed to reasonably consider all of their personal circumstances warranting special relief from citizenship revocation.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant admits false representations but argues analyst failed to consider personal circumstances for relief, court reports.

propositions.text: Application for judicial review is dismissed for reasons that follow.
propositions.quote: For the reasons that follow, this application is dismissed.

paragraphs.summary: Court dismisses the application for judicial review, court states.

propositions.text: Applicant was born in Fiji on January 23, 1961.
propositions.quote: The Applicant was born in Fiji on January 23, 1961.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant was born in Fiji on January 23, 1961, court states.

propositions.text: Applicant was convicted in Fiji of larceny in October 1977 and criminal trespass in November 1979.
propositions.quote: In October 1977, the Applicant was convicted in Fiji of larceny. In November 1979, the Applicant was convicted of criminal trespass in Fiji.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant was convicted in Fiji of larceny in 1977 and criminal trespass in 1979, court states.

propositions.text: Applicant attended University of Canberra 1987-1990, committed sexual offence in April 1989, left Australia before trial, traveled to Canada 1990-1991.
propositions.quote: The Applicant attended the University of Canberra in Australia from 1987 to 1990, completing a Bachelor of Environmental Science. In April 1989, the Applicant committed the offence of sexual intercourse without consent. The Applicant left Australia prior to trial. They travelled to Canada in January 1990, for one year and then returned to Fiji in 1991.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant attended University in Australia, committed sexual offence, left before trial, traveled to Canada 1990-1991, court states.

propositions.text: Applicant married current wife in Fiji on January 15, 1994, and adopted her two children.
propositions.quote: On returning to Fiji, the Applicant met their current wife whom they married on January 15, 1994. The Applicant later adopted their wife’s two children.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant married current wife in Fiji in 1994 and adopted her two children, court states.

propositions.text: Fiji extradited Applicant to Australia in December 1994; convicted March 8, 1995; sentenced to over two years; removed to Fiji February 18, 1997 after imprisonment.
propositions.quote: In December 1994, Fiji extradited the Applicant to Australia to face the criminal charge. On March 8, 1995, the Applicant was found guilty of the charge and received a prison sentence of two years and two months plus an additional term of nine months which was to expire on November 16, 1997. The Applicant was removed to Fiji on February 18, 1997 at the completion of their term of imprisonment.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant extradited to Australia, convicted, sentenced, and removed to Fiji after imprisonment, court states.

propositions.text: Applicant applied for Canadian visitor visa Dec 8, 1999, falsely declared no criminal offences or residence over six months elsewhere.
propositions.quote: On December 8, 1999, when applying for a temporary resident visa to Canada as a visitor, the Applicant declared that they had never committed a criminal offence in any country. In doing so, the Applicant failed to disclose their criminal convictions in Fiji and Australia and attested to not having lived in any other country for more than six months in the past five years despite having been incarcerated in Australia for 26 months.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant falsely declared no criminal offences or long residence abroad in 1999 Canadian visitor visa application, court states.

propositions.text: Applicant applied for permanent residence Feb 2000, failed to disclose convictions, residence, studies in Australia; submitted various supporting documents.
propositions.quote: In February 2000, the Applicant applied for permanent residence in Canada under the assisted relative (other) class. The Applicant failed to disclose the criminal convictions in Fiji and Australia or that they had been ordered to leave Australia. The Applicant also omitted the fact that they had attended university in Australia and had resided there from 1987 to 1990 and from 1994 to 1997. Supporting documents accompanying the application included birth certificates for six children, adoption orders for two children, birth certificates for the Applicant and their wife, as well as their marriage certificate and divorce orders for each of their previous spouses.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant applied for permanent residence in 2000, failed to disclose convictions and residence in Australia, submitted supporting documents, court states.

propositions.text: Applicant disclosed Fijian convictions in Oct 2000 immigration interview but not Australian conviction or residence in Australia.
propositions.quote: In October 2000, the Applicant attended an immigration interview in Australia. At that time, the Applicant disclosed the Fijian convictions, but did not disclose the conviction in Australia for non-consensual sexual intercourse. Nor did the Applicant disclose that they had resided in Australia.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant disclosed Fijian convictions but not Australian conviction or residence in Australia in 2000 interview, court states.

propositions.text: Immigration officer found Fijian convictions did not affect admissibility due to juvenile status and no Canadian equivalent offence.
propositions.quote: The immigration officer determined at the end of the interview that the Fijian convictions did not affect the Applicant’s admissibility because the Applicant was a juvenile at the time of the first one and the second offence had no Canadian equivalent.

paragraphs.summary: Immigration officer found Fijian convictions did not affect admissibility, earlier decision-maker found.

propositions.text: Permanent residence application approved Nov 23, 2001; Applicant and family landed in Canada.
propositions.quote: The application for permanent residence was approved on November 23, 2001 and the Applicant, together with their wife and eight children landed in Canada.

paragraphs.summary: Permanent residence approved Nov 2001; Applicant and family landed in Canada, earlier decision-maker found.

propositions.text: Applicant and wife had another child in September 2002.
propositions.quote: In September 2002, another child was born to the Applicant and their wife.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant and wife had another child in September 2002, court states.

propositions.text: Applicant applied for Canadian citizenship January 2005; approved November 29, 2005; Applicant and family took oath and became citizens.
propositions.quote: In January 2005, the Applicant applied for Canadian citizenship. It was approved on November 29, 2005, at which point the Applicant took the oath of citizenship and became a Canadian citizen. The Applicant, their wife and the eight children born outside of Canada all became Canadian citizens that day.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant applied for citizenship in 2005; approved; Applicant and family became citizens, court states.

propositions.text: On July 19, 2007, Canada Border Services Agency received info from Australia and Interpol about Applicant's conviction and movements, forwarded to IRCC.
propositions.quote: On July 19, 2007, Canada Border Services Agency received information from the Australian government and Interpol disclosing the Australian conviction and the Applicant’s record of movement. This information was forwarded to IRCC.

paragraphs.summary: In 2007, Canada Border Services received and forwarded to IRCC info on Applicant's Australian conviction and movements, court states.

propositions.text: IRCC issued Notice of Intent to Revoke Citizenship on October 7, 2015, on ground of misrepresentation; Applicant applied for judicial review.
propositions.quote: On October 7, 2015, the IRCC issued to the Applicant a Notice of Intent to Revoke Citizenship on the ground of misrepresentation. The Applicant applied for judicial review of the Notice of Intent.

paragraphs.summary: IRCC issued Notice of Intent to Revoke Citizenship in 2015; Applicant applied for judicial review, earlier decision-maker found.

propositions.text: In Hassouna, 2017 FC 473, revocation process found null and void for violating Canadian Bill of Rights.
propositions.quote: On May 10, 2017, in Hassouna v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2017 FC 473 [Hassouna], Madam Justice Gagné, as she was at the time, found the existing revocation process to be null and void because it violated the Canadian Bill of Rights, SC 1960, c.44.

paragraphs.summary: Hassouna decision found revocation process null and void for violating Canadian Bill of Rights, court reports.

propositions.text: As a result of Hassouna, Citizenship Act was amended by Bill C-6 after Strengthening Canadian Citizenship Act.
propositions.quote: As a result of the decision in Hassouna, the former Citizenship Act, which had been amended by the Strengthening Canadian Citizenship Act, SC 2014, c 22, [hereafter, the SCCA] was further amended with the passage of Bill C-6.

paragraphs.summary: Following Hassouna, Citizenship Act was amended by Bill C-6 after prior amendments, court states.

propositions.text: The Act received Royal Assent on June 19, 2017, and the Applicant's Notice of Intent to Revoke was cancelled on July 10, 2017.
propositions.quote: On June 19, 2017, the Act received Royal Assent. On July 10, 2017, the October 7, 2015 Notice of Intent to Revoke the Applicant’s citizenship was cancelled.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Act received Royal Assent on June 19, 2017, and the Applicant's Notice of Intent to Revoke was cancelled on July 10, 2017.

propositions.text: The changes to the citizenship revocation process came into effect on January 24, 2018.
propositions.quote: The changes to the citizenship revocation process came into effect on January 24, 2018.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the citizenship revocation process changes took effect on January 24, 2018.

propositions.text: On July 17, 2018, a Request for Information letter was sent to the Applicant, who did not respond.
propositions.quote: On July 17, 2018, a Request for Information letter was sent to the Applicant. Ultimately, no response was made to the letter.

propositions.text: IRCC initiated revocation procedures by issuing a Notification Letter on January 2, 2019, outlining the Applicant's chronology and decision to initiate revocation.
propositions.quote: The IRCC initiated revocation procedures by issuing a Notification Letter dated January 2, 2019. The Notification letter outlined the Applicant’s chronology of facts in detail and advised that the Delegate had decided to initiate revocation proceedings.

paragraphs.summary: The court states a Request for Information was sent July 17, 2018, with no response; IRCC issued a Notification Letter January 2, 2019, to start revocation.

propositions.text: On March 4, 2019, the Applicant provided extensive written submissions, a personal affidavit, and supporting documents.
propositions.quote: On March 4, 2019 the Applicant provided extensive written submissions and a personal affidavit with a great number of supporting documents as evidence to support the submissions.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Applicant submitted extensive written submissions and affidavit with evidence on March 4, 2019.

propositions.text: Sections of the Act referred to are set out in the attached Appendix for ease of reference.
propositions.quote: For ease of reference, the sections of the Act referred to herein are set out in the attached Appendix.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the relevant Act sections are in the attached Appendix for reference.

propositions.text: On August 27, 2020, the Delegate concluded on a balance of probabilities that the Applicant obtained citizenship by knowingly concealing material circumstances.
propositions.quote: on August 27, 2020, after reviewing the submissions, the Delegate concluded that they were satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that the Applicant had obtained Canadian citizenship by knowingly concealing material circumstances about their residence, post-secondary studies, and conviction in Australia.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Delegate concluded August 27, 2020, that the Applicant obtained citizenship by knowingly concealing material facts.

propositions.text: The Delegate found the Applicant deliberately withheld information about a sexual assault conviction to obtain permanent resident status, undermining immigration integrity.
propositions.quote: The deliberate withholding of information regarding the Applicant’s past criminal conviction for sexual assault in order to obtain permanent resident status was found to strike at the integrity of Canada’s immigration program.

propositions.text: The Delegate held the Applicant’s establishment in Canada was insufficient to warrant special relief.
propositions.quote: The Delegate held that the Applicant’s establishment in Canada was insufficient to warrant special relief.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Delegate held the Applicant deliberately withheld conviction info, undermining immigration integrity, and establishment did not warrant relief.

propositions.text: The Applicant’s citizenship was revoked under subsection 10(1) of the Act.
propositions.quote: The Applicant’s Canadian citizenship was revoked under subsection 10(1) of the Act which is set out later in these reasons.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Applicant’s citizenship was revoked under subsection 10(1) of the Act.

propositions.text: The Delegate recognized the Applicant lived in Canada over 20 years, worked various jobs, furthered education, and was involved in the community.
propositions.quote: The Delegate recognized that the Applicant had lived in Canada for a significant time period, over 20 years, and had worked various jobs, furthered their education, and was involved in the community.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Delegate recognized the Applicant’s long residence, work, education, and community involvement in Canada.

propositions.text: The Delegate acknowledged the Applicant’s close relationship with children and grandchildren and their support.
propositions.quote: The Delegate acknowledged that the Applicant has a close relationship with their children and grandchildren and that they provide them with financial and emotional support, advice, and encouragement.

propositions.text: Little weight was given to rehabilitation submissions because the Applicant did not take responsibility for fraudulent acts.
propositions.quote: Little weight was given to the Applicant’s submissions regarding rehabilitation because they had not taken responsibility for their fraudulent acts during the immigration and citizenship process.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Delegate acknowledged family ties but gave little weight to rehabilitation as Applicant did not accept responsibility.

propositions.text: The Delegate found the Applicant’s submissions did not show how revocation would directly harm their children, focusing on removal impact instead.
propositions.quote: The Delegate found that the Applicant’s submissions did not support how revocation of their citizenship would directly cause their children harm because the submissions focused primarily on the possible impact of being separated from their family upon removal.

propositions.text: The Delegate held these submissions were premature as the issue was revocation, not removal, and should be addressed in removal proceedings if any.
propositions.quote: The Delegate held that these submissions were premature as the sole issue of the proceedings was revocation of citizenship. The Delegate stated that the submissions would be more properly addressed at subsequent removal proceedings, should they take place.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Delegate held the Applicant’s harm submissions premature and more appropriate for removal proceedings.

propositions.text: The Delegate found the Applicant’s medical condition and Fiji’s medical care submissions similarly premature.
propositions.quote: The Delegate also found the Applicant’s submissions regarding their medical condition, need for medical treatment, and Fiji’s allegedly inadequate medical care to be similarly premature.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Delegate considered medical condition submissions premature as well.

propositions.text: The parties agree the issue is whether the Decision is reasonable.
propositions.quote: The parties agree that the issue is whether the Decision is reasonable.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the parties agree the issue is the reasonableness of the Decision.

propositions.text: The parties and court agree the standard of review is reasonableness based on Vavilov presumption.
propositions.quote: In that respect they also agree, as do I, based on the presumption in Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65 [Vavilov], that the standard of review for citizenship revocation decisions is reasonableness.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the parties and court agree the standard of review is reasonableness per Vavilov.

propositions.text: The parties differ on what factors the Delegate should consider to reach a reasonable Decision evaluating the Applicant’s submissions.
propositions.quote: Where the parties differ is as to what factors the Delegate should consider in order to arrive at a reasonable Decision when evaluating the Applicant’s submissions.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the parties differ on what factors the Delegate should consider for a reasonable Decision on Applicant’s submissions.

propositions.text: The Delegate did not properly interpret section 10 of the Act by failing to consider the Applicant’s personal circumstances.
propositions.quote: The Applicant submits that is the major issue in this application. Within that, the Applicant argues that the Delegate did not conduct a proper interpretation of section 10 of the Act when they did not consider the personal circumstances of the Applicant.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant argues the Delegate failed to properly interpret section 10 by not considering personal circumstances.

propositions.text: Consideration of the Applicant’s circumstances was premature as revocation does not automatically trigger removal.
propositions.quote: The Respondent submits that consideration of the Applicant’s circumstances was premature as all that happened was a loss of citizenship status and citizenship revocation does not automatically trigger removal.

paragraphs.summary: The Respondent argues consideration of Applicant’s circumstances was premature since revocation does not automatically cause removal.

propositions.text: It was reasonable for the Delegate to consider personal circumstances based on the Act’s provisions.
propositions.quote: The Respondent also submits that in considering section 10 of the Act, it was reasonable for the Delegate to consider the personal circumstances of the Applicant on the basis set out in the Act.

paragraphs.summary: The Respondent argues the Delegate reasonably considered personal circumstances as allowed by the Act.

propositions.text: The Applicant did not deny making misrepresentations; section 10.2 presumes citizenship obtained by fraud if permanent resident status was obtained by fraud.
propositions.quote: The Applicant did not deny that they had made misrepresentations. Section 10.2 of the Act creates a presumption, for the purposes of subsection 10(1) and 10.1(1), that a person has obtained their citizenship by false representation or fraud or by knowingly concealing material circumstances if the person becomes a permanent resident by one of those means, and because of having acquired the status of a permanent resident, they subsequently obtained citizenship.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Applicant admitted misrepresentations and section 10.2 presumes citizenship obtained by fraud if permanent resident status was fraudulent.

propositions.text: Justice Gagné in Hassouna found personal interests and humanitarian factors should be part of procedural fairness in citizenship revocation.
propositions.quote: In Hassouna, Justice Gagné evaluated the constitutionality of the administrative model for “non-complex” citizenship revocation cases on grounds of fraud or misrepresentation. Justice Gagné found that “consideration of personal interests or humanitarian and compassionate [H&C] factors should form part of the procedural fairness offered to affected individuals by the citizenship revocation process”: paras 2 and 124.

propositions.text: Both the Applicant and their eldest son were applicants in Hassouna.
propositions.quote: In this respect, I note that both the Applicant and their eldest son were applicants in Hassouna.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes Justice Gagné in Hassouna ruled personal and humanitarian factors are part of procedural fairness; Applicant and son were applicants there.

propositions.text: The Act requires the Minister to refer cases for citizenship revocation unless personal circumstances warrant special relief.
propositions.quote: the Act provides that the Minister shall refer a case to the court for revocation of citizenship for false representation, fraud, or knowingly concealing material circumstances unless “considerations respecting the person’s personal circumstances warrant special relief in light of all the circumstances of the case”

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Act mandates referral for citizenship revocation unless personal circumstances warrant special relief.

propositions.text: Whether the Delegate erred by finding consideration of foreign hardship and children's best interests premature.
propositions.quote: The issue here is whether the Delegate erred in finding consideration of potential foreign hardship and the best interests of the Applicant’s children was premature and not to be included in the Decision’s analysis.

paragraphs.summary: The court identifies the issue as whether the Delegate erred in finding consideration of foreign hardship and children's best interests premature.

propositions.text: The Delegate did not err in finding consideration of foreign hardship and children's best interests premature.
propositions.quote: For the reasons that follow, I find the Delegate did not err in this regard.

propositions.text: Did the Delegate err in finding consideration of foreign hardship and children's best interests premature?
propositions.quote: A. Did the Delegate err in finding the consideration of potential foreign hardship and the best interests of the Applicant’s children was premature?

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes the Delegate did not err in finding consideration of foreign hardship and children's best interests premature and frames the issue.

propositions.text: Applicant argues for humanitarian and compassionate considerations including children's best interests, health issues, and establishment in Canada.
propositions.quote: the Applicant put forward several reasons for the Delegate to apply humanitarian and compassionate considerations to their situation. These were: the best interests of the Applicant’s children and grandchildren the Applicant’s significant health issues and the lack of access to adequate health care in Fiji the Applicant’s establishment and rehabilitation in Canada

paragraphs.summary: The applicant argues for humanitarian considerations including children's best interests, health issues, and establishment in Canada.

propositions.text: Section 7 Charter not engaged at inadmissibility stage; inadmissibility distinct from removal.
propositions.quote: the Federal Court of Appeal has noted “there is extensive case law establishing that an inadmissibility finding is distinct from effecting removal and that, as other steps remain in the process, a finding of inadmissibility does not automatically or immediately result in deportation”

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker found section 7 Charter not engaged at inadmissibility stage; inadmissibility distinct from removal.

propositions.text: Applicant ceased citizenship under subsection 10(1) and became inadmissible under IRPA for misrepresentation.
propositions.quote: On ceasing to be a citizen under subsection 10(1) of the Act, the Applicant fell under paragraph 40(1)(d) of the IRPA which states that a foreign national is inadmissible for misrepresentation.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the applicant ceased citizenship and became inadmissible under IRPA for misrepresentation.

propositions.text: Non-citizens do not have an unqualified right to enter or remain in Canada.
propositions.quote: “the most fundamental principle of immigration law is that non-citizens do not have an unqualified right to enter or remain in Canada”: Hassouna at para 154 citing Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration) v Chiarelli, [1992] 1 SCR 711 at 733.

propositions.text: Applicant is a foreign national after citizenship revocation.
propositions.quote: The Applicant is present in Canada and their change of status rendered them a foreign national.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the applicant is a foreign national and non-citizens lack unqualified rights to remain in Canada.

propositions.text: Applicant does not have right to appeal to Immigration Appeal Division after citizenship revocation.
propositions.quote: As a foreign national whose citizenship has been revoked for misrepresentation, the Applicant does not fall within any of the categories of persons who may appeal to the Immigration Appeal Division, as set out in Division 7 of the IRPA.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the applicant cannot appeal to the Immigration Appeal Division after citizenship revocation.

propositions.text: Applicant argues likely to depart Canada due to lack of appeal and status, citing IRPA paragraph 40(2)(a).
propositions.quote: The Applicant argues that without a right of appeal and without citizenship or permanent resident status, it is foreseeable that they are likely to depart Canada, whether voluntarily or involuntarily. It is submitted that this is evidenced by paragraph 40(2)(a) of the IRPA which states that a “foreign national continues to be inadmissible for misrepresentation for a period of five years following, […] in the case of a determination in Canada, the date the removal order is enforced”

paragraphs.summary: The applicant argues they are likely to depart Canada due to lack of appeal and status, citing IRPA provisions.

propositions.text: Court disagrees that IRPA reference to 'is enforced' guarantees removal of Applicant.
propositions.quote: I cannot agree that a reference in the above-noted section of the IRPA to the words “is enforced” shows that there will definitely be a removal of the Applicant.

paragraphs.summary: The court disagrees that IRPA's 'is enforced' phrase guarantees the applicant's removal.

propositions.text: Applicant has remedies under IRPA and IRPR to prevent removal, including Temporary Resident Permit and humanitarian grounds.
propositions.quote: The range of remedies available to the Applicant to prevent removal are found not in the Act but rather in the IRPA and the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations SOR/2002-227 [IRPR]. For example, the Applicant can apply under section 24 of the IRPA for a Temporary Resident Permit. If removal proceedings are commenced, the Applicant can apply for a stay of removal under section 50. Under section 25(1) they may apply to the Minister on humanitarian and compassionate grounds on the basis set out in section 233 of the IRPR. The Minister may stay a removal order against a foreign national if they are of the opinion that the stay is justified by humanitarian and compassionate considerations under subsection 25(1) or 25.1(1) or by public policy considerations under subsection 25.2(1) of the IRPA. The Applicant may also seek a pre-removal risk assessment under section 112 of the IRPA which may stay the removal order if any of the conditions in section 232 of the IRPR apply.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the applicant has remedies under IRPA and IRPR to prevent removal, including humanitarian grounds.

propositions.text: Respondent argues Act provisions should not be conflated with IRPA provisions and context matters.
propositions.quote: The Respondent submits that the provisions of the Act should not be conflated with those of the IRPA. The Respondent also reminds the Court that context is important.

paragraphs.summary: The respondent argues the Act's provisions should not be conflated with IRPA's and context is important.

propositions.text: Court agrees with respondent that Act and IRPA provisions should not be conflated.
propositions.quote: I agree.

paragraphs.summary: The court agrees with the respondent that the Act and IRPA provisions should not be conflated.

propositions.text: Delegate considers personal circumstances for relief from citizenship revocation; no evidence of deportation proceedings.
propositions.quote: The Delegate is to consider the Applicant’s personal circumstances with a view to whether or not to grant relief from revocation of citizenship. While the Applicant placed their possible removal before the Delegate for consideration, there is no evidence in the underlying record that deportation proceedings had been initiated or were contemplated.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Delegate considers personal circumstances for relief; no evidence deportation proceedings started.

propositions.text: Applicant notes phrase 'all the circumstances of the case' was interpreted in Chieu under Immigration Act.
propositions.quote: The Applicant points out that the phrase “all the circumstances of the case” in paragraph 10(3.1)(a) of the Act was also found in the Immigration Act, RSC 1985, c.I-2, the scope of which was interpreted by the Supreme Court of Canada in Chieu v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) 2002 SCC 3 [Chieu].

paragraphs.summary: The applicant notes the phrase 'all the circumstances of the case' was interpreted in Chieu under the Immigration Act.

propositions.text: Chieu considered whether Immigration Appeal Division could consider foreign hardship in removal appeals for permanent residents.
propositions.quote: Chieu considered whether the Immigration Appeal Division was entitled to consider potential foreign hardship when dealing with appeals of removal orders made against permanent residents.

paragraphs.summary: Chieu considered if Immigration Appeal Division could consider foreign hardship in removal appeals for permanent residents.

propositions.text: Supreme Court in Chieu broadly interpreted 'all the circumstances' to include conditions faced upon removal.
propositions.quote: The Supreme Court determined that “having regard to all the circumstances of the case” is to be broadly interpreted as the words appear in a provision establishing a discretionary jurisdiction and there is no detailed guidance as to how the discretion is to be exercised. The Court found that use of the word “all” in the context suggests that the greatest possible number of factors relevant to the removal of a permanent resident from Canada be considered and that it was evident that one such factor is the conditions an individual would face upon removal: Chieu at paras 29 and30.

paragraphs.summary: The Supreme Court in Chieu broadly interpreted 'all the circumstances' to include conditions faced upon removal.

propositions.text: Applicant submits Chieu's logic should apply to the Act.
propositions.quote: The Applicant submits that the same logic should apply to the Act.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant submits that Chieu's logic should apply to the Act.

propositions.text: Court disagrees that Chieu applies to the Act; facts and context differ and conflating Act and IRPA is improper.
propositions.quote: I disagree that Chieu is applicable in this instance. It does not address any aspect of the Act. It is factually different in that it dealt with a provision of the Immigration Act, and a removal order against a permanent resident. There is no removal order against the Applicant and they are a foreign national, not a permanent resident. The Applicant’s submission, if accepted, would have the effect of conflating the Act and the IRPA.

paragraphs.summary: The court disagrees that Chieu applies to the Act, noting factual and contextual differences and risk of conflation.

propositions.text: Applicant submitted Senate Committee transcript on Bill C-6, which became the Act.
propositions.quote: In addition to Chieu, the Applicant submitted a transcript of the proceedings of the Standing Senate Committee on Social Affairs, Science and Technology, which took place on March 1st, 2017, to study Bill C-6, which subsequently became the Act.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant submitted a Senate Committee transcript on Bill C-6, which became the Act.

propositions.text: Minister and staff assured Senators that personal circumstances consideration includes humanitarian and compassionate factors
propositions.quote: the Minister and staff administering the legislation assured the Senators that consideration of an Applicant’s personal circumstances would include humanitarian and compassionate factors

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker found that the Minister and staff assured Senators that personal circumstances consideration includes humanitarian and compassionate factors.

propositions.text: Delegate found submissions on children's best interests focused on removal impact, distinct from citizenship revocation
propositions.quote: the Delegate found that the “submissions regarding the best interests of the children and grandchildren should you be removed from Canada are premature and would be more properly addressed at subsequent removal related proceedings

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker found submissions on children's best interests were premature and related to removal, not citizenship revocation.

propositions.text: Delegate's finding that considering children's best interests was premature is reasonable
propositions.quote: The Delegate’s finding that it was premature to consider the best interests of the children and grandchildren is reasonable

propositions.text: Section 10(3.2) requires Minister to consider representations before decision
propositions.quote: The provision in section 10(3.2) that “the Minister shall consider any representations received pursuant to paragraph (3.1)(a) before making a decision” occurred

propositions.text: Delegate considered Applicant's personal circumstances but Applicant disagrees with outcome
propositions.quote: The Delegate was required to consider the Applicant’s personal circumstances and they did so. The Applicant simply disagrees with the outcome

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Delegate reasonably considered children's best interests premature, complied with section 10(3.2), and considered personal circumstances though Applicant disagrees.

propositions.text: Delegate acknowledged Applicant's heart failure and medical reports without dispute
propositions.quote: The Delegate acknowledged that the Applicant had health concerns, most notably heart failure. The Delegate said they had read the medical reports and did not dispute the information they contained

propositions.text: Delegate found Applicant could apply for medical insurance if removal proceedings initiated; health issues better assessed then
propositions.quote: the Delegate found that if removal proceedings were initiated the Applicant could apply for medical insurance to purchase their prescription medications and receive medical treatment, and as removal is a separate proceeding, the health issues would be better assessed at the removal proceeding

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker acknowledged Applicant's heart failure and found health issues better assessed at removal proceedings with possible medical insurance.

propositions.text: Applicant challenges Delegate's statement as speculative and unrealistic given financial situation
propositions.quote: The Applicant challenges that statement as being speculative and unrealistic given the financial situation of the Applicant

propositions.text: Delegate's finding that health issues better assessed at removal proceeding was rationale for prematurity finding
propositions.quote: The finding that those issues would be better assessed at a removal proceeding was the rationale for the finding that the health issues were premature

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant argues Delegate's health assessment is speculative; court finds Delegate's prematurity finding was based on removal proceeding rationale.

propositions.text: Delegate noted Applicant's establishment in Canada was due to misrepresentation to obtain permanent residence and citizenship
propositions.quote: I note that your level of establishment in Canada may not have been attained had you not been granted permanent residence status...based off of the fact that you misrepresented yourself to obtain permanent residence, and subsequently Canadian citizenship

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker found Applicant's establishment in Canada resulted from misrepresentation to obtain status and citizenship.

propositions.text: Applicant argues discounting establishment due to misrepresentation contradicts jurisprudence and undermines relief protection
propositions.quote: They say that such an approach would hollow out the nature of a request, as almost every requestor, by definition, has benefited from a past immigration violation...it would have the effect of hollowing out the protection that was deliberately enacted by Parliament

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant argues discounting establishment due to misrepresentation contradicts jurisprudence and undermines relief protection.

propositions.text: Respondent says Applicant merely disagrees with Delegate's consideration and weighing of establishment
propositions.quote: The Respondent submits that the Applicant is simply disagreeing with the manner in which the Delegate considered and weighed their establishment

paragraphs.summary: The Respondent submits Applicant only disagrees with how Delegate weighed establishment.

propositions.text: Respondent points out Delegate considered establishment in light of misrepresentation seriousness and late disclosure
propositions.quote: The Respondent points out that the Delegate considered the establishment factors in light of the seriousness of the misrepresentation and the failure to come forward with it until 2019

paragraphs.summary: The Respondent points out Delegate considered establishment factoring misrepresentation seriousness and late disclosure.

propositions.text: Semana case holds establishment under illegal circumstances should not be rewarded
propositions.quote: Justice Gascon found there is nothing unreasonable in a conclusion that establishment under illegal circumstances should not be rewarded

propositions.text: Persons should not benefit from immigration law circumvention or duplicity
propositions.quote: it is trite law that persons ought not to benefit from their circumvention of immigration laws and their wanton duplicity in their immigration applications

propositions.text: Applicants cannot be rewarded for time in Canada without legal right
propositions.quote: applicants cannot and should not be 'rewarded' for accumulating time in Canada, when in fact, they have no legal right to do so

paragraphs.summary: The Semana case holds illegal establishment should not be rewarded and persons should not benefit from immigration law circumvention.

propositions.text: IRPA requires good faith and compliance for settlement; public interest supports considering this
propositions.quote: IRPA and the Canadian immigration regime are founded on the principle that whoever comes to Canada with the intention of settling must be of good faith...There is clearly a public interest consideration at stake

paragraphs.summary: IRPA requires good faith and compliance for settlement; public interest supports considering this in decisions.

propositions.text: Applicant denied criminal convictions in 1999; enjoyed benefits of misrepresentation for 19 years
propositions.quote: Applicant first denied having any criminal convictions in December, 1999...For approximately 19 years, the Applicant enjoyed the benefits of their misrepresentation

propositions.text: Delegate reasonably gave little weight to Applicant's rehabilitation due to late responsibility
propositions.quote: It was reasonable for the Delegate to take that into consideration and find that the Applicant’s rehabilitation was deserving of little weight as the Applicant failed to come forward and take responsibility for their acts until they received the Notification Letter in 2019

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Applicant denied convictions and benefited from misrepresentation for 19 years; Delegate reasonably gave little weight to rehabilitation.

propositions.text: Delegate's establishment analysis is reasonable given facts and jurisprudence
propositions.quote: I find on the facts of this matter, and in light of the jurisprudence, that the Delegate’s establishment analysis is reasonable

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Delegate's establishment analysis reasonable based on facts and jurisprudence.

propositions.text: Delegate's conclusions on prematurity of foreign hardship and children's best interests are reasonable
propositions.quote: I also find that the Delegate’s conclusions that it was premature to consider any potential foreign hardship and the best interests of the Applicant’s children if the Applicant is removed to be reasonable

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Delegate's conclusions on prematurity of foreign hardship and children's best interests reasonable.

propositions.text: Reasonableness review focuses on decision made, not what court would decide or de novo analysis
propositions.quote: The focus of reasonableness review must be on the decision actually made by the decision maker...a court applying the reasonableness standard does not ask what decision it would have made...conduct a de novo analysis or seek to determine the “correct” solution

paragraphs.summary: The court states reasonableness review focuses on the decision made, not the court's own decision or de novo analysis.

propositions.text: Reasonable decision displays justification, transparency, intelligibility focused on actual decision
propositions.quote: a reasonable decision is one that displays justification, transparency and intelligibility with a focus on the decision actually made

propositions.text: Reasons under review display justification, transparency, intelligibility
propositions.quote: I find the reasons under review display these characteristics

paragraphs.summary: The court states reasonable decisions display justification, transparency, intelligibility; finds reasons under review do so.

propositions.text: Reasonable decision is internally coherent, rational, justified by facts and law
propositions.quote: a reasonable decision is one that is based on an internally coherent and rational chain of analysis and that is justified in relation to the facts and law

propositions.text: Reasons under review meet coherence, rationality, justification requirements
propositions.quote: I find the reasons under review also meet these requirements

paragraphs.summary: The court states reasonable decisions are coherent, rational, justified; finds reasons under review meet these requirements.

propositions.text: Decision is reasonable; Delegate's reasoning justified, intelligible, transparent without fallacies
propositions.quote: I find that the Decision is reasonable. The Delegate’s reasoning is justified, intelligible and transparent without any logical fallacies or incoherent reasoning

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes the Decision is reasonable and Delegate's reasoning is justified, intelligible, and transparent.

propositions.text: Application is dismissed
propositions.quote: The application is dismissed

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the application.

propositions.text: Parties acknowledged no notice of certified question given, thought it could be addressed at hearing
propositions.quote: At the outset of the hearing of this application the parties acknowledged that they had not given notice of a certified question as they were under the impression that one could be addressed at the hearing

paragraphs.summary: The court notes parties acknowledged no notice of certified question was given, mistakenly thinking it could be addressed at hearing.

propositions.text: They indicated that they each had a version of a possible certified question.
propositions.quote: They indicated that they each had a version of a possible certified question.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker noted that each party had a version of a possible certified question.

propositions.text: I agreed to allow the parties to consider whether a possible certifiable question arises after release of this Judgment and Reasons.
propositions.quote: I agreed to allow the parties to consider, following release of this Judgment and Reasons, whether a possible certifiable question, or questions, arise on the facts.

paragraphs.summary: The court agreed to let parties consider if a certifiable question arises after judgment release.

propositions.text: Parties must discuss within four working days whether serious questions of general importance arise for certification.
propositions.quote: The parties are to discuss, within four working days of release of this Judgment and Reasons, and determine whether they believe any serious question or questions of general importance arise for certification.

propositions.text: If so, proposed questions must be filed with proof of service in PDF and Word by the seventh working day after judgment release.
propositions.quote: If so, then the proposed question or questions are to be filed with the Court, with proof of service, in both PDF and Word format, no later than close of business of the Vancouver Registry Office on the seventh working day after release of this Judgment and Reasons.

paragraphs.summary: The court ordered parties to discuss certification questions within four days and file proposed questions by the seventh working day.

propositions.text: Each party must file submissions on proposed questions within seven working days after filing the questions, limited to four pages.
propositions.quote: Submissions of each party with respect to any such proposed question or questions shall be filed with the Court, in both PDF and Word format, with proof of service, no later than close of business of the Vancouver Registry Office within seven working days of the submission of the proposed question or questions.

propositions.text: Submissions may be single-spaced and must not exceed four pages.
propositions.quote: Submissions may be single-spaced and shall not exceed four pages in length.

paragraphs.summary: The court ordered parties to file submissions on proposed questions within seven days, single-spaced and max four pages.

propositions.text: Any reply submissions must be filed within three working days of receipt, single-spaced and max two pages.
propositions.quote: Any submissions in Reply shall be served and filed, in both PDF and Word format, single-spaced, not exceeding two pages in length no later than close of business of the Vancouver Registry Office within three working days of receipt of the submissions.

paragraphs.summary: The court ordered reply submissions to be filed within three days, single-spaced and max two pages.

propositions.text: The application is dismissed.
propositions.quote: The application is dismissed.

propositions.text: The question of certification is reserved pending review of submissions and proposed questions.
propositions.quote: The matter of whether there is a question or questions to be certified is reserved pending receipt and review of any such question or questions and written submissions from the parties.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismissed the application and reserved the certification question pending submissions.
